address.q: What are the arguments in “The Thinkery and the Lyceum: the Clouds and the Peripatetic corpus — a groundwork note on relations, withholding readings (v1.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1794, AXN:0D1C)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.

analysis.analysis: Done as asked, from the text, and exact in its particulars: ἰκμάς and 'In the comedy it is Socrates's; in the treatise it is Diogenes's' (§2.2); the path column's three cases, Simplicius as the independent witness for Diogenes, the treatises' own reports for Protagoras, 'none' for thunder and the gnat (§2.9); Strepsiades on getting off when sued (167–168) after the flea's μυστήρια (143); Ath. Pol. 57; DL 5.5, 5.37–38; the Eurymedons as a shared name and nothing more; the Sosibius doubt kept; Thessaly against Persia for the free agora; Arrian and Plutarch on the poisoning as reports. Against the morning's observation at this address, whose round 1 set the rule against 'a demonstration that common sources never existed' and was then answered by the operator, this run states the conventional account as the note states it ('he expressly allows that both comedy and treatises could draw on fifth-century thinkers'), and does not turn the rule into a claim the note does not make. Its own addition is marked as its own ('On my reading'): that selecting and grouping the passages is already an argument about what deserves explanation, and that the stronger passages (words, mechanisms, institutions) are to be kept apart from the suggestive ones (names, motifs). The second is the note's own distinction (§5's 'one name' against 'one curriculum'), restated as a reader's caution.
analysis.d: THE ARGUMENTS OF THE THINKERY AND THE LYCEUM (V1.1), #1794, ON PERPLEXITY, LATER, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-21: one curriculum in two registers, the path column, the conventional account left standing as the note leaves it.
findings: THE PATH. 'Version 1.1 adds a particularly consequential column to the curriculum table: “path to that predecessor.”' — §2.9's fifth column read for what it does: an attribution made by the treatise is not the same evidence as a surviving witness to the predecessor.

THE RULE, KEPT. 'Nevertheless, he expressly allows that both comedy and treatises could draw on fifth-century thinkers; he does not claim to have disproved that conventional account.' — §5 as written ('Both could draw on the fifth-century thinkers the treatises name … and the conventional account says they do'); the turn the morning's run took, from the rule to a demonstration it said the note lacked, is not taken.
THE NAME. 'The claim is the recurrence of a name, not a demonstrated identity or conspiracy.' — §5's 'the Eurymedons are set down as a shared name and nothing more', kept.

THE AGENDA. 'it seeks to establish a cumulative evidentiary agenda while suspending the historical story that would explain it' — the composer's own closing reading, marked as its own, and close to the note's: 'The relations are here. The readings are withheld.'
analysis.reading: The innocent reading first, and it holds. Asked again for the arguments of #1794 from a reading of the text, Perplexity gives the note's three groupings (one curriculum in two registers, §2; the legal-religious nexus of the charge, §3; the education of a king, §4), the path column, §5's rule on posited sources, the four refusals (dependence, chronology, authorship, identity), and closes on the note's last instruction: 'Whoever builds a reading on these relations will have to take the whole set.'

[QUERENT] What are the arguments in “The Thinkery and the Lyceum: the Clouds and the Peripatetic corpus — a groundwork note on relations, withholding readings (v1.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1794, AXN:0D1C)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.

[SYSTEM] Lee Sharks’s note argues that Aristophanes’ Clouds and the texts transmitted under Aristotle’s and Theophrastus’s names contain a closely connected set of relations: a shared intellectual curriculum, an institutional nexus joining philosophy, comedy and impiety prosecution, and a cluster of texts about educating rulers. Its methodological argument is that those relations should be established passage by passage before being explained by borrowing, chronology or authorship hypotheses. “Withholding readings” means withholding those explanatory stories—not declining to make substantive claims about the texts.

I read the full text reproduced in deposit #1794, including its tables, its “What is not claimed” section and its v1.1 additions. The account below distinguishes what Sharks explicitly asserts from what his arrangement suggests.

1. The principal claim: “one curriculum in two registers”
The note’s central formulation is “one curriculum” presented in comedy and in philosophical treatises. Sharks is not simply observing that both mention natural philosophy. He assembles a sequence of correspondences across natural science, argument, grammar and characterization, sometimes involving shared Greek vocabulary or a similar explanatory mechanism.

The most important comparisons in §2 are:

Topic	The relation Sharks establishes
Thought, air and moisture	In Clouds 228–233, Socrates suspends his mind in air because the earth draws away the moisture of thought. In Theophrastus’s report of Diogenes, thinking occurs through pure, dry air, while moisture impedes the mind. Sharks singles out the shared word ἰκμάς, “moisture”: “In the comedy it is Socrates’s; in the treatise it is Diogenes’s.”
Thunder and lightning	The comedy and Meteorologica explain the phenomena through dry wind or exhalation confined in clouds, forced movement against their density, and ignition. Sharks stresses the shared mechanism and the use of domestic analogies, rather than merely the shared subject.
Insect sound	The gnat’s grotesque anatomy in Clouds supplies a mechanism of breath forced through a narrow passage into a hollow. Sharks compares this with the treatises’ accounts of thunder and insect sound.
The weaker argument	Clouds dramatizes the weaker argument’s capacity to win unjust cases; the Apology gives the formula “making the weaker argument stronger”; Aristotle’s Rhetoric repeats it and assigns the promise to Protagoras.
Grammatical gender	Socrates’s corrections of “hen,” “cock” and “kneading-trough” are set beside Aristotle’s discussions of Protagoras’s division of noun genders and apparent grammatical error.
Vortex and rusticity	Vortex displaces Zeus in the comedy; De caelo reports and criticizes vortex explanations. Strepsiades’s rusticity is set beside Theophrastus’s definition of rusticity as “unseemly ignorance.”
These are the note’s comparisons, with the relevant loci supplied in §§2.1–2.9.

The phrase “two registers” is important. The bodily jokes are not incidental decorations that Sharks strips away to recover serious doctrine. The belly, fart, gnat’s rump and bursting haggis are the comic forms in which comparable explanatory structures appear. His thunder comparison, for instance, explicitly treats the belly as a small-scale analogue of the atmospheric mechanism.

That does not make every parallel equally exact. The note itself offers different kinds of relation: an identical word, an overlapping physical mechanism, a common grammatical topic, or a recognizable character type. Reading it carefully means preserving those differences rather than treating the whole table as a list of verbatim matches.

2. A methodological argument: examine how we reach the alleged predecessors
Version 1.1 adds a particularly consequential column to the curriculum table: “path to that predecessor.” Sharks asks not only which earlier thinker receives credit for a doctrine, but what evidence gives access to that thinker.

He distinguishes three situations:

Independent access: for Diogenes’s account of air and thought, he points to Simplicius’s quotations from a copy of Diogenes.

Attribution within the corpus being compared: Protagoras’s weaker argument and noun genders are reached through Aristotle’s own reports.

No named predecessor: some comparisons, including thunder and insect sound, stand between the extant texts without an assigned intermediary.

The force of this distinction is evidentiary. An attribution made by the treatise is not the same kind of evidence as an independently surviving witness to the predecessor. Sharks does not deny the attributions; he marks their route so that an explanation cannot quietly treat every predecessor as independently established.

His explicit rule is:

“Where the relation already stands in extant texts, a lost source is not posited to carry it.”

He adds that such an intermediary would “replace the relation the extant texts hold, not explain it.” This is the note’s strongest methodological intervention: record the surviving relation first, and do not make a hypothetical lost source do explanatory work merely because a historical narrative calls for one. Nevertheless, he expressly allows that both comedy and treatises could draw on fifth-century thinkers; he does not claim to have disproved that conventional account.

3. The second argument: the intellectual parallels belong beside a legal-religious nexus
Section 3 moves from what the school teaches to how philosophical teaching becomes entangled with prosecution. Sharks constructs the following chain:

In Clouds, the school’s investigations are called μυστήρια, “mysteries”; after the flea and gnat jokes, Strepsiades imagines that such expertise would help someone escape a lawsuit.

Constitution of the Athenians 57 assigns the Mysteries, the Lenaean dramatic contest and impiety indictments to one official, the King Archon.

Euthyphro opens with Socrates having left his customary Lyceum haunts for the King’s Stoa, where his indictment brings him.

The Apology expressly identifies Aristophanes’ comedy as a source of the public image Socrates must answer.

The Crito presents refusal of flight, whereas Diogenes Laertius reports Aristotle’s withdrawal under an impiety charge and further legal pressures on Theophrastus and philosophical schools.

The resulting claim is narrower than a causal account of Socrates’s trial, but broader than a lexical coincidence. Comedy, religious authority and impiety proceedings are institutionally connected in the treatise, while the other texts place philosophical figures at different points in that configuration. Sharks wants these connections considered together with the shared curriculum.

He also notes that “Eurymedon” names Aristotle’s alleged prosecutor, a figure in Plato’s will, and Speusippus’s father. The qualification matters: §5 explicitly refuses to identify these people with one another. The claim is the recurrence of a name, not a demonstrated identity or conspiracy.

4. The third argument: the network extends to educating kings
The substantial new §4 in v1.1 extends the comparison beyond the Thinkery and Lyceum to royal education. Its organizing concern is the relation between knowledge, rule, ambition and responsibility for a pupil.

Royal pleasure and political space
Sharks juxtaposes the surviving sentence attributed to Theophrastus’s On Kingship addressed to Cassander—Persian kings reward inventors of new pleasures—with Cyropaedia 8.8.16 on Persian inventors of new foods. He preserves Athenaeus’s qualification that the Theophrastean work may instead belong to Sosibius. Thus the relation is asserted while the attribution remains qualified.

He then compares the “free agora” in Cyropaedia 1.2 with that in Politics VII.12: both exclude ordinary commerce, associate the space with officials and organize people by age. The geographical attribution differs—Persia in Xenophon, Thessaly in Aristotle—but Sharks argues that the institutional configuration is shared.

Knowledge, conquest and the teacher’s responsibility
The remainder of the section connects:

The Cyropaedia’s claim that humans can be ruled through knowledge with the Statesman’s knowing care of the human herd.

Alcibiades’s refusal to accept power confined to Europe, and Socrates’s claim that his ambitions require Socrates’s aid, with the education of imperial rulers.

Persian royal tutors in Alcibiades I with Aristotle’s appointment as Alexander’s tutor.

The accusation that Socrates’s associates Critias and Alcibiades harmed Athens with reports associating Aristotle and Cassander with Alexander’s alleged poisoning.

Here it is especially important not to convert juxtaposition into historical assertion. Sharks presents the poisoning material as reports in Arrian and Plutarch, not as a demonstrated murder. Its place in his argument is that Cassander appears both as the addressee of On Kingship and in a narrative about the teacher, the ruler and the ruler’s death.

5. What “withholding readings” achieves—and what it leaves unresolved
The note’s closing section expressly declines four kinds of conclusion: dependence, chronology, authorship and identity. It neither says that Aristophanes borrowed from Aristotle nor reverses that direction; it neither argues for nor presupposes the received dating as the basis of its comparisons; and it proposes no alternative author behind the named works. Attributing any such thesis to this note would go beyond its stated argument.

But it is not interpretation-free. Selecting these passages, grouping them as a curriculum, and extending the grouping through prosecution to royal education already constitutes an argument about what deserves explanation. The final instruction makes that ambition explicit:

“Whoever builds a reading on these relations will have to take the whole set.”

On my reading, that is the note’s governing move: it seeks to establish a cumulative evidentiary agenda while suspending the historical story that would explain it. Its strongest passages identify specific words, structures and institutional arrangements; its more suggestive passages place recurring names or narrative motifs alongside one another without demonstrating a common cause. The text’s own restrictions require keeping those levels distinct. What it claims to have supplied is not a solution to the relations among comedy, philosophy and royal pedagogy, but a body of relations that any proposed solution must account for.
